utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday, 18th of June, 2008. Good afternoon, witness, good afternoon to the accused, the Defence counsel, the OTP representatives and all the people helping us out. First of all I'm going to give the floor to my fellow Judge and then Mr. Karnavas, you may be able to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody, I would like to make an observation which is not of a personal character, I have spoken to my colleagues, and we all share the same view. It is also not specifically addressed to Defence 1, Mr. Karnavas, but to all parties, but the immediate reason is the hearing of this witness and rather than the hearing, the way the documents that are presented to him are put at the disposal of the Chamber. You must have noticed that we are constantly turning around, fiddling with documents, I am the most lucky of us all because I have an empty chair and I can sort of line them up whereas the president has to reach underneath. It is not just that it is a physical exercise that is not the best fitness training although it may have an element of that, but it does not serve your cause because often we just find the document when you call the next one so that we cannot do much with it and one almost is tempted to suspect, but I do not say so, but one is almost tempted to suspect that you do not want us to read them, which I please do not want to be taken seriously; but I chose where this leads, so I think the Chamber would greatly appreciate if you could give us the documents in the way that you have them yourself and you have them presented to the witness. It would make our work easier and yours more effective. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I appreciate that observation. I did notice it yesterday, particularly that -- we will try to rectify that. It is not intentionally it's sometimes that not until very late Sunday night that we have rearranged it. It's -- just so you know, Your Honours, the way we prepare our documents is that we look at -- we have them in a chronological order. We go through them and then depending on the number of documents, I rearrange them at the last moment and -- in order to fit the time constraints, but I do recognise the problem; and I assure you that we will try to not let this happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I expected this response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- if I may proceed, Mr. President, I have another -- I have a matter to raise with the particular document and this is document 1D 02940, hard copies have been provided to everyone. It hasn't been -- it has not been released into e-court. Yesterday at some point as a result of the ongoing conversations, I asked someone in the United States to locate Dr. Silajdzic's actual presentation before the Senate back then, and I was able to get a fax -- it was faxed to me late last night. Recognising that this is a new document, I would nonetheless wish to proceed by asking a couple of questions. It's nothing is -- nothing is new concerning the -- we saw the letters but I do wish to bring out a couple of points to the witness's attention especially but not exclusively a response by Mr. Izetbegovic to one of Mr. Akmadzic's letters to Mr. Biden, so with the Court's permission I would like to put a few questions to this witness. So I'm seeking permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor. Do you have any observations or reservations?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I -- the Prosecution realizes how these things happen and we have no objection to be used in this instance there might be different circumstances at different times, but on this occasion we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look at 1D 02940. It has been put before you. We spoke yesterday about you being in New York. We see from the very first page of the document it is dated February 18, 1993. This is the testimony or the statement by Haris Silajdzic the then foreign minister before the subcommittee on European Affairs of the Committee of the Foreign Relations. Now, if you could go to page 50, will you see towards the middle of the page, I think it's notice third paragraph, I will read, it says: "Tragically negotiations in the name of peace have facilitated the intensification of war. The reason for this is very simple. Instead of responding to naked aggression, the United Nations sponsored peace process has increasingly delivered a series of concessions and awards to the aggressor." Now this was the foreign minister speaking on behalf of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you share this observation that Dr. Silajdzic was making before the Senate subcommittee?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not share those views. I received this paper now and the Presidency as a whole did not share those views. All of us in the Presidency were unanimous that under the auspices of the international peace conference on the former Yugoslavia or the London conference as it was called that we should continue with the talks and continue trying to find a solution for peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to another segment. This would be on page -- I believe it's 59. 59 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I take the floor. Frankly, I -- when I listen to the witness' statement now, I wonder if the witness is aware of the fact that then, Dr. Silajdzic mainly referred to the Serb aggression and the next paragraph says that, and I quote, "That the hope beyond the process would seem to have been that if enough concessions were given, the aggressor would be satisfied." I mean if enough concessions would be given by the United Nations, it means, then the aggressor would have been satisfied. So I don't know if the witness has -- of course he didn't have the chance to read this whole chapter and parts of it but he may be given the time to have a look at that and then to answer your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is the disadvantage of not having the document earlier, and I don't wish to telegraph anything because you do have to look this entire statement and then look at what Boutros Boutros-Ghali was saying and what Lord Owen was saying and you will see where it all fits in but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may use this seeming pause to go a bit on in the same direction. Later on in the paragraphs of this page, Mr. Silajdzic speaks of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That -- what do you say to this, Witness, Mr. Akmadzic? Do you find yourself reflected when he says, "The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina unconditionally agreed to these negotiations ..." for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that sometimes the government and the Presidency sometimes as it is in the American system where the government is the head of state in a way, that Mr. Silajdzic actually equates the two, and let me go back to what I said before. The international conference here in a way rewards the aggressor. Of course I'm opposed to that, but as far as those negotiations are concerned, they -- everybody had equal status there. Nobody was rewarded for anything, and we were treated in an equitable manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a nicely precise and direct answer to my question. Just to be sure, what is referred to, according to you by the words "the aggressor"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case, and in general, in the documents that we have at our disposal, the term "aggressor" always refers to the Serb side or as the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina defined the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the aggression of Serbian Montenegro, Yugoslavia, and the JNA; and we called it the internal aggression. That is a term as we noted at the time that did not exist in any other war and that's the organised formations of the Serb side within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party, the interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you go to page 59, the third paragraph from the bottom, he's asked a question by Mr. Biden: "Please describe your country's make-up, the maybe-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina for me, not necessarily in percentages but in terms of ethnic composition and why do you believe you can put it back together again?" This is what Dr. Silajdzic says, "Well, Bosnia and Herzegovina is an old country. We all used to be Bosnians. We used to be called Bosnians Catholic, Catholics, Muslims, and orthodox." Senator Biden "Catholics, orthodox and Muslims." Dr. Silajdzic says, "Yes, and Jews. Those are the four groups of people that actually built Bosnia, all Bosnia. Bosnia used to be a big Balkan kingdom that comprised big parts of Croatia and Serbia, never vice versa." Now, Mr. Akmadzic, at that point in history, are we talking about a Bosnia where you have -- where there are people identified as Bosnians and there just happen for particular religious denomination, Catholics, orthodox, Jewish or Muslim? And is Dr. Silajdzic correct in his answer to Senator Biden?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Silajdzic's answer to Senator Biden is not correct. Let me point out two or three things. First, of all the Bosnian kingdom as such ceased to exist in 1463, I think, after the Turkish occupation. During the existence of the kingdom that he's talking about and the greatest Bosnian king was King Tvrtko, our opinion today is that he was a Catholic, that he was a Croat, although we don't know what his aloud affiliation was. We think that he died in 1391 so in late 14th century, in the period that is of interest for this Honourable Trial Chamber and for us, Bosnia and Herzegovina has three sovereign peoples, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. In World War II at the very end of the war, there was a big assembly. A decision was made for Bosnia and Herzegovina -- that Bosnia and Herzegovina was not Serbian, Croatian, or indeed Muslim. The decision was that it belonged to all three peoples. It was Bosnian -- Croatian, Muslim, and Serbian. The Muslim people was recognised as such in the amendments to the Yugoslav constitution passed in 1974, and it was recognised as the Bosniak people at the Washington negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at page 96 now, it's the very last page. Yesterday, we saw two of your letters that you sent to Senator Biden and we also saw Senator Biden's declaration or response. Here, we find attached as part of the record a letter submitted by Mr. Izetbegovic and so I want to go with this -- go over this very quickly. It's the very last page, sir, do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see that the -- it's dated February 25th, 1993, and it says here: "Dear Senator Biden, this is to inform you that my term as president of the Presidency was extended beyond December 24, 1992 under the constitutional provisions allowing for the extension of the term due to the 'emergency situation.' This was done by the approval of the Presidency as a whole." Is that true or is it false?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed this with the Judges of the Constitutional Court because I'm not a lawyer myself, and the constitution says that in war and if the state of war has been declared, the president and the members of the Presidency have their term of office extended, but it is also quite obvious that this refers to the members of the Presidency and that they are the ones who have to elect from among their number the president in accordance with the rules of procedure of the Presidency and in the rules of procedure, the term of office is limited strictly to one year, plus another year. And this means that in this letter, President Izetbegovic is not right and it is in particular not correct that the entire Presidency agreed with that because that is simply not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So let me be more direct. Is this a true or a false statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is really a statement made by the president because he signed it but his words are not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we go on. It says, "The Presidency represents the Croats, Muslims, Serbs ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Karnavas, but really it is a very important matter. So the -- this issue has come up many times already in this Chamber and we -- I mean the Chamber and the Judges would like to see really how things happened and transpired. Now, frankly, we would like to see some written confirmation of either of the views, who was there, any decision recorded by the transcripts of the Presidency, or there was none. It is my question and I hope that we will find an answer either by the Defence or by the Prosecution, but we have to have a look at the documents themselves. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As far as we know, Judge Prandler, and that's a very good question, and try as we might, we were unable to find those records because as we understand it, those records of those days vanished. They are no longer in the archives. And I leave it to the members of the Trial Chamber to determine where they may be or what happened to them. But we can ask the gentleman whether he presided -- whether he was present during any meetings where they decided, based on an emergency situation, to prolong Mr. Izetbegovic's term as president. That may assist us, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, can you help us here?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before leaving for the Geneva talks that started on the 2nd of January, 1993, sometime around the 17th or 18th of December, 1992, a few days before the second term of office of President Izetbegovic expired, I discussed this with him. I warned him that he was given a second year in office thanks to the votes of the Croat members in the Presidency and that it was now the turn for a Croat to become the president of the Presidency because in accordance with the rules of the procedure of the Presidency; so we're not talking about the constitution at all but the rules of procedure of the Presidency, he does not have the right to extend his term of office for another year. And he told me, We'll talk about it in Geneva. And I warned him that once we were in Geneva, that would be ten days or so after the expiry of his term and he said, I will discuss this with Tudjman. And I told him, You have two Croat members of the Presidency here. I as the prime minister at that time, it is our decision to make, not Tudjman's. He told me, The army would not allow me to step down as the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could -- unless there is a -- you have a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just perhaps for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I find it surprising that we have here the transcript of a hearing of February 18, and we have attached letters that are of a later date which I find a bit strange but maybe it's -- I just want to have it on the record that we have noted, and it is a bit surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe Judge Trechsel, in the document that I showed you with Mr. Biden's response, he said that he would make it part of the record of the hearing. And I should note that the actual record is about 90 to 100 pages long, this is just the excerpt concerning Dr. Silajdzic's testimony for this whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: According to the paper I have, the last page of the hearing is page 66 where it says, "That the public meeting was concluded."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. I -- again, I had somebody going to the Philadelphia library yesterday to pick this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Actually it was on page 94 that the hearing was concluded at 5.55 p.m. but still on the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. But -- and I haven't worked up on the hill, but as I understand, and we can see this from Senator Biden's response that he indicated that he would make Mr. Akmadzic's letter that he received after the hearings part of the record; and so I can only suspect that since this is all part of this whole hearing, that's why we have the series of letters because you also have Mr. Akmadzic's letter on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have seen that. When did Mr. Biden make such a statement that he would put this in the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may have -- if I may have the indulgence of the Court for one moment. Your Honours, 1D 02847. This was dated February 25th, 1993, a question concerning the Bosnian government. It was a week ago "One week ago the European subcommittee held a day-long hearing on the subject of American policy in Bosnia." Then it talks about Silajdzic. Then it says, "Yesterday, I received a letter from the prime minister of Bosnia, Mile Akmadzic." As I understand it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The next sentence is " ... which I will make part of the record."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. That's where my memory was slipping. Yeah, because I know for a fact that he indicated and I know how the Senate works a little bit because this is a part of the appendix. If you note on page 95, Your Honours, this is part of the appendix, so this would have been part and parcel of those hearings because obviously Mr. Akmadzic challenged what the foreign minister was saying and also brought to the attention that Izetbegovic was not the president of the Presidency because his mandate had run out. Now, if we would go to the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I have not intervened so far. I looked at the document with great interest and I noted that the meeting took place in the SD 562 room of the American Senate and ended at 1629. At 1643, there is another speaker, General Odon. Normally he was to speak to the military aspects of the situation in the former Yugoslavia, so you had the beginning of his hearing; but the rest is missing and then we go straight to page 94. It might have been good to know what that General said then. Maybe there's no connection at all with this witness but I noted that in passing. I just wanted to convey it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I did notice that, Mr. President, in my haste when I sent my note my contact to go to the library and search for this document, I specifically asked for the statement by Dr. Haris Silajdzic and he was -- it's not on the internet so he was able to -- he just copied and faxed the portion, but I can certainly make available the entire proceedings which I said I believe is about 90 pages long, that's what I was told somewhere in that vicinity; but that would not be a problem, and I can have that done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the middle of the paragraph going on, the middle of the letter, says, "The Presidency represents" -- going back to the last page, I'm still reading of Mr. Izetbegovic's letter, it says: "The Presidency represents the Croats, Muslims, Serbs and the others in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In addition, all of the members of the Presidency, including myself, continue to hold office under the original mandates by which they took office." Is that true or false? My timing is very limited, Mr. Akmadzic.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time Mr. Izetbegovic is talking about is the time when the two Serb members had already left the Presidency. Another two came along who had not been elected. Their legitimacy was questionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So is it true or false?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: False.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we go on: "Alija Izetbegovic says Dr. Haris Silajdzic is the official head of the delegation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the ongoing talks sponsored by the conference on the former Yugoslavia now underway in New York. His testimony before your committee is entirely of the position of the republic and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Is that true or false?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: False.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, just to -- you were the prime minister, Haris Silajdzic was the foreign minister so he would have been under you as part of the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that a minister can be led by a prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Was Dr. Haris Silajdzic a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And by the way, one final question: Were you ever served with a copy of this letter that President Izetbegovic sent to Senator Biden?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go back to our documents, we'll need the binder, and we'll pick up where we left off yesterday that's with 1D 02314. Again we left off on the issue of Medjugorje and that agreement. So this would be in binder 1. Again to bring to everyone's attention, yesterday we saw from Lord Owen's book on 1D 02037 we saw that as of May 26th, a foreign officer by the name of Douglas Hogg was trying to get Mr. Owen to acknowledge that the VOPP was dead, I mention that highlight May 26th because this document here, 1D 02314 is 27 May 1993, and here this is addressed to a particular legal advisor. And if you look at the very first paragraph, it says: "Lord Owen wants to convene a working group of lawyers who represent all the sides in the coordinating body as soon as possible in Geneva." Do you see that, sir? It's in paragraph number 1. Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at document 1D 02314, if we could have the assistance of the usher to help the gentleman find the document. Okay. You will see under paragraph number 1, it says: "Foreseeing the meeting of the coordinating body which had been agreed in Zagreb on 24 April and pencilled in for Friday, 4 June, Lord Owen wants to convene a working group of lawyers who represent all sides in the coordinating body as soon as possible in Geneva." Do you have that text, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether the lawyers did meet based on this in order to draft any legislation?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, 1D 02322. This is in binder 1, Your Honours. And this is dated 30 May 1993. It's a public announcement. It's from the Croatian Muslim Democratic Party and here it says that they are in the middle of the paragraph, it says, "We see the light in accepting the implementation of said agreements with a strong and permanent union with the Croats." And we see further down where certain people are recommended. Do you see where the five individuals being recommended starting with Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the -- do you know who the Croatian Muslim Democratic Party is?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Muslim Democratic Party is a Muslim party. Muslims, for the most part, living in Zagreb, but some of their members were in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This party was not in agreement with the SDA, the party in power, the party that won the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 02468. It's in binder number 2, Your Honours. This is dated 31 May 1993. If you could please look at it. Have you found the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just look at it because I'll be referring to it. This is a letter to Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg by Mate Boban where -- and this is in reference to an invitation for a meeting in Sarajevo and essentially Mate Boban is saying, in paragraph 2 that is: "Any new meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic would be superfluous and would mean the continuation of the practice of avoiding the implementation of what has already been agreed on." Can you please explain what Mr. Boban is saying here, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference is here to the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic had consistently been failing to implement any agreements. Among other things, the coordination body had never met and had never taken over the function that had been agreed previously at Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, 1D 02904, the very next document. It's in binder 3, Your Honours, and I can assure you this will not happen again. I will make sure we have it. 1D 02904. These are minutes of a meeting of the members of the Presidency of RBiH dated June 15, 1993. The minutes were taken by Mr. Trnka, and we see that your name is there in the very first paragraph along with Mr. Boras's name. Were you present during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at the second paragraph it says: "The participants were given draft decree laws (in English) on 1, a coordinative body for implementation, establishing provinces and their bodies, ombudsmen, a court for human rights, international instruments for the protection of human rights, and cooperation with the monitoring mission for human rights ..." and so on and so forth. Now, do you recall ever being given drafts?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got those. They were distributed to us they meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think due to time we'll move to the next document unless the Court has any questions with respect to this document. I should ask you, on paragraph number 3, it does say: "Before commencing discussions on the offered drafts, Ejup Ganic requested that the situation of Gorazde be considered since it was critical so that the aggression might be stopped." Can you please explain what Mr. Ganic is trying to do here?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ganic is trying and succeeding in a way of postponing the adoption of decisions. He imposes a condition here that normally we, during negotiations, would not have considered a condition for the continuation of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a minute. We also find on the fourth paragraph Lord Owen pointing out that this was a consulting meeting. So it was not a meeting that was supposed to take to lead to decisions, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lord Owen is right as far as that is concerned, but Lord -- no specific conclusions Lord Owen believed no specific conclusions but negotiations were underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the meeting had nothing to do with Gorazde which was nowhere near where the Croats and the Muslims are involved in in their discussions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no HVO in Gorazde. This was no reason for us and Muslims to discuss this except if maybe trilaterally as part of the overall process we decided to bring it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in keeping with what we just saw, I'm going to show you several documents, and I just need confirmation. 1D 02407. The next few documents, Your Honours, are in binder number 2. This is the BH Presidency proposal on decree laws on provinces. So early in this meeting in Geneva when they were talking about handing over draft decree laws, this is what we are talking about; correct? This is one of them?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at 1D 02408, we have a draft decree law from the ombudsman 's office; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then if we look at 1D 02409, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 02409. This is a decree law on the Court of human rights of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Another draft decree is 1D 02410. This is on the adoption of international instruments for the protection of human rights?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Next document 1D 02411. Draft decree law on cooperation with the international monitoring mission for human rights. That's 1D 02411; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. These are all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These were all the texts that were being discussed at that -- these were all draft texts being discussed, correct, as part of the negotiating process?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then we go to 1D 02412. Decree law on military council of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then I think it's the last one, I believe this is the last one, maybe not. 1D 02413. We have a decision to appoint members of the military council of BiH, and we see your name there. Was this part of the negotiating process?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 01940. This is in binder 1, Your Honours. 1940. If you could just look at the document while everybody is getting these, trying to locate it. This is minutes from the session of the RBH Presidency held in Geneva on 16 June 1993. We see in the very second page that your name is there along with Boras. So were you at that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at item number 2, we see it says: "In order to implement Vance-Owen Plan as much as possible, the co-chairmen of the peace conference on the former Yugoslavia propose the following six draft laws." And that was the -- those were the laws that we saw; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you go to page number 2, we see your name a couple of times. The first paragraph, it says, "Akmadzic said that they thought that the Vance-Owen Plan had not failed." That was your understanding at that time; correct? Is this correct that you still were hopeful?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's not just that I wasn't and there were other hopes that we were entertaining too although we were witnessing increasingly quite a different approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the second paragraph is interesting, it says, "Akmadzic felt that the coordinating body should appoint a prime minister-elect of the interim government of RBH." And I believe that we already saw a document early on where Dr. Jadranko Prlic had been appointed prime minister. Can you give us an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained adamant regardless of --, I remained adamant that Dr. Jadranko Prlic be appointed prime minister, as had been agreed in Medjugorje on the 18th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we go further down and we see Silajdzic, he said that: "There was no point in discussing the proposed decrease if the Vance-Owen Plan was being abandoned. These documents cannot be discussed and adopted with reference to the Vance-Owen Plan when we don't even know what exactly it implies." To your understanding, at that point in time, were you, as a member of the negotiating team, aware that the Vance-Owen Plan was being abandoned?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was assuming that its implementation depended on our will, whether we would accept it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Then we see Mr. Izetbegovic where he says: "That it was difficult to explain it to accept that the side which does not acknowledge BH and which is has not signed the plan should be part of the higher state organs. It is unacceptable that the coordination body has the character of a state organ and then it can adopt binding decisions." Could you please explain what Izetbegovic is saying here because I thought there was already an agreement, coordinating body had been formed. Where is Izetbegovic saying here?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izetbegovic is adamant in backing the status quo in order not to have a coordination body in order not to have a new prime minister appointed. And he is also adamant that the Serb side should not be part of the coordination body because in his very words, they were the aggressors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to page 3, we see the conclusions and the last conclusion says: "The Presidency stands by the support for the Vance-Owen Plan but its readiness to implement it -- and that it is open for further talks." Now was that a correct statement? Was that a conclusion that was actually reached? Because we have Silajdzic saying that it's being abandoned here, there is support for it. Izetbegovic, we said signed on to this coordinating body, now he doesn't agree with it. So can you please explain this conclusion because it's rather confusing?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our conclusion was that the talks were still very much along the lines of the Vance-Owen Plan regardless of the fact that not everyone agreed as to what stage the negotiations were actually at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at item number 5, it says that: "The Presidency sent the proposal by the Croatian Democratic Union submitted by Mr. Akmadzic to launch procedures for the appointment of Ante Cuvalo for ambassador to -- of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United States." May I ask whether Mr. Cuvalo was appointed to the ambassador to the United States pursuant to your initiative or the initiative of the Croatian Democratic Union, which was obviously accepted by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was normal for the parties to provide the initiative. We did, the Presidency took that on board. Despite this, Mr. Cuvalo was never appointed ambassador to Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. There is -- the next document, 1D 02840. Binder number 3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is an announcement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can I be heard now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is an announcement pursuant to the request of the co-chairmen of the peace conference he says: "On the former Yugoslavia and the conclusions reached at the meeting in Geneva on 16 June 1993 during the previous weekend representatives of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna met with representatives of the Muslims and Serb side with the aim of coming to an agreement on the new proposals for the resolution of the crisis of BH. In separate talks with the high representatives of the other two peoples in BH, Mr. Mate Boban and his associates expressed the Croatian view of the future arrangement of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." did that happen? Were you part of this process?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it says here, and it would appear that based on this announcement that you are -- and I'm saying you, the Croat delegation along with the Muslim and the Serb delegation are being prompted by the co-chairmen of the peace conference; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we're going to go to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you still have some ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's going to be a Herculean effort, but we'll see what we can do. If we go to 1D 02664. This is in binder number 2, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, I would really be most grateful if we could be as quickly as possible and as efficient. Of course I share the blame for this confusion in the courtroom so ... We see this is a tape recording of the Presidency, of a Presidency meeting on the 29th June, 1993. Have you had a chance to look at this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact if we go through it, we see that you are present at the time and you make several observations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, yesterday or the day before, you made a reference to a Mr. Fikret Abdic who had complained about Mr. Delic --

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we can find it in this particular transcript; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And because we can read it, and we can see who said what, it would appear also that there was some complaints towards Mr. Izetbegovic in that he was using his position without informing other members of the Presidency and that was an observation made by Mr., I believe, Lasic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. For the record, you were, that can be found on pages 9 and 10 of the document. Okay. Now, we can go on to the next document. I apologise to the Court for not being able to spend more time on this. It was rather self-explanatory, the minutes, that is, the tape recording. If we go to the next document, 1D 02309 it's in binder number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you have the document, sir? 1D 02309. It's -- we see --

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's dated 1 July 1993 and this is addressed to the General Secretary of the UN, and you are commenting, we can see on the very first paragraph about an attack that commenced on 30th of June, 1993 in the town of Mostar. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you do express and opinion in paragraph number 4, you say: "The objective of this aggression is to impede the implementation of the already existing peace agreements prevent further development of the peace process, and postpone talks on the future political structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Could you please tell us very briefly what happened on June 30th, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the time when the Muslim forces attacked both in Mostar and in Central Bosnia. This is the time when reached the water shed point with the Vance-Owen Plan which was not being implemented. This is the time when the failure to accept the Vance-Owen Plan and lack of knowledge on the part of the Muslim party means the increasing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just draw your attention to the fact that I have now found the document in binder number one and not in binder number 2 as you had indicated. So I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't feel that I can be blamed. I did not -- I was not able to follow at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. This is part of the problem with these time constraints but as I indicated, Your Honours, we will try to put it all in order. We've hired extra staff. We're doing it both on electronic version and manually. And I think in the future we will have to hire more staff to do that. You can imagine how difficult it is to read this stuff, put it together. It would be helpful to tell the registry to give us more funding for this. Anyway ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now that we have the letter, can you briefly tell us again very briefly what happened on June 30th? Please speak slowly, so we have your full answer in the record.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, the Muslim forces in Mostar launched an attack on the HVO and the Croatian people in Mostar. And they stepped up the attacks in Central Bosnia. These attacks had started in April and continued afterwards, and we warned about the fact that the Muslim party is hesitant to accept international negotiations. In this specific case we're talking about the Vance-Owen Plan and that it is trying to force some other decisions to be taken by those aggressive tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 01937. This is now 11 July 1993. Binder number 1, 1937. This is a letter to the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it's a statement actually. It begins by saying: "At a session held in Zagreb, 11 July 1993, chaired by Presidency member Dr. Ejup Ganic, the Presidency of the republic of BH discussed and further elaborated the draft of the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Then we see towards the bottom of the page that we have I guess what would be the draft constitutional order. If we go to page number 2 under paragraph 9, we see that it calls for: "The BH constitution is adopted as part of an international conference. The constitution of federal units to be adopted by each of them may not contravene the BH constitution or decisions of the Constitutional Court." Then lastly, I just want to point out if I ask you the question on page 3, we see under Roman numeral II: "The principles for constituting federal units: 1, the federal units cannot be constituted on an exclusively ethnic basis. 2, nature and geography, the economy, traffic, culture, and tradition will be taken into consideration in constituting federal units." I believe you were asked a question -- I think it was by Judge Trechsel yesterday concerning your vision of how this should be constituted. Was this your understanding keeping in mind that we may be discussing a different peace plan here?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, regardless of what the peace plan was, it was our constant position that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be organised as a decentralized state based on the criteria that are listed here, not only in ethnic terms but ethnic, geographic, cultural, historical, and all the other elements must be included. Bosnia and Herzegovina is recognised as a sovereign state, but it consists of the constituent units and constituent peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go back to page 1. We see Lord Owen and we see Stoltenberg's name. Is this their initiative or is this the initiative of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a new plan that started with Owen and Stoltenberg but the criteria remained the same. The criteria for the setting up of the units and the only difference is how the units were formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Go on to the next topic and I just need a few moments, Your Honours, and I believe I'm going to be through rather quickly. The next binder for the gentleman and we're going to be looking at a document. We will be looking at the -- at a document and it's P 05051. That's your first document. This would be in binder number 4, Your Honours. P 05051. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You've seen this document before in this courtroom. It's dated September 14, 1993, it's a joint declaration between President Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic and if you look at under Roman numeral 2, it talks about the formation of working groups and then if we look at page number 3, we see that President Franjo Tudjman appointed as a trustee, Dr. Mate Granic, and President Alija Izetbegovic appointed Dr. Haris Silajdzic. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, based on this joint declaration, were you involved in any working groups?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved in the work of one of the groups, and that was the group for the reduction of tensions between the two peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the reason behind this joint declaration, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we saw that the war, and the war in Central Bosnia in particular was continuing and that in spite of our orders, it was not stopping and we tried to find a solution in some other way. The Muslim side in Bosnia and Herzegovina or rather they wanted to deal with the Republic of Croatia more than they wanted to deal with us, the representatives of the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that is why two representatives were appointed, one by Franjo Tudjman and the other by Alija Izetbegovic who would continue being in constant contact and the establishment of the working groups was yet another way, another effort to solve the problems that could not be solved up until that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, my fellow Judges are telling me that your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I would, with the Court -- with the Court's indulgence, I would ask for the remainder of the period. I understand that we asked for six hours, and if I can't, I would at least like to read into the record the documents that I would have shown in conjunction with this topic and they're not that many but they're all based on this last answer, based on the working groups. So -- I can understand if the Court feels we should move on, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many documents are you going to mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The documents that I have I don't really need to discuss too much, you were, because they are part of this working group process. It's 1D 02837, 2898, 2897, 2899, 2900, and I believe it's 1291, 1D 01291. They're all basically -- then 2876, these are all based on these working groups to show that this was an ongoing process. Then lastly, I did wish to have the gentleman discuss one part of his transcript which the Prosecution may probably bring up and that's on P 07260, this is the presidential transcript of 19 December 1993 on page 24. I'm sure it hasn't been -- hasn't escaped Mr. Scott's eyesight, and I certainly didn't want to think that we were somehow avoiding to ask the tough questions and then lastly, there was one document, 1D 01556 from the -- it's from the Balkan Odyssey but actually this was a communication that was submitted, if the time is up, then I will be moving these documents in by way of a motion. I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Because you probably saw the documents with the witness, who saw them together with you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I think it is best to have a break now since it's 3.30, and then I'll turn to the Defence counsel and the other Defence teams to ask them whether they have questions. So let's have a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I shall now ask Ms. Nozica whether she has questions for the witness. There's nobody for the 1D Defence. Here they come. Ms. Nozica, do you have questions? But before I ask you for that to be recorded in the transcript, the Trial Chamber by way of an oral ruling decided that document 1D 02940 would be added to the 65 ter list. So I think it's clear. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before Ms. Nozica takes -- I just wanted to thank the witness. I didn't get an opportunity to thank the witness, and I just wanted to make sure that Mr. Akmadzic recognises that we do thank him very, very much for coming here and giving his evidence; and we really appreciate his frank answers in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence 2 has some questions but my colleague, Madam Alaburic is going to begin first and then I will follow with my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence 3 does not have any questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 4D?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, good afternoon to you, good afternoon to Mr. Akmadzic, to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Akmadzic, I am Vesna Alaburic, I am an attorney-at-law from Zagreb, and I'm representing General Milivoje Petkovic in this case. First of all, I would like to provide an explanation about my cross-examination to the Trial Chamber, and I would like to ask you, Mr. Akmadzic, to listen carefully because then you will have an idea as to what I would like to get from you. In the examination in chief where Mr. Karnavas showed to the witness a note, presidential statement from the Security Council where the HVO is described as I quote: "Paramilitary formations of the Bosnian Croats," which gave rise to a letter of protest that this witness wrote to the Security Council -- to the president of the Security Council, I would like to ask this witness some questions about the HVO as an element of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina with equal status with the other elements. The other topic will have to do with the transcript of the meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date is the 26th of December, 1992. The number is 1D 2663. This was shown to the witness yesterday, and I am interested in the part of this transcript or minutes where Sefer Halilovic talks about his deputy, Jovo Divjak an ethnic Serb asking -- or rather discussing whether he was under arrest at that time or not, and I would like to ask the witness to comment on his intervention as it was recorded in the minutes. So, sir, I think that it will not take us longer than 10 or 15 minutes. First of all we'll talk about the HVO as component of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday and this is recorded in your document 1D 2096 that you said to the president of the Security Council that the HVO was a legitimate army recognised by the government and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the document 1D 2664, there's no need for you to go looking for it because I will read all the relevant portions to you, this is the document that can be found in the second binder. It is the minutes from the meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date is the 29th of June, 1993. This is what you are recorded as saying, Mr. Akmadzic. The date was about the issue whether General Rasim Delic was a member of the Presidency ex officio because he was the chief of the general staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina and you said at page 9 in the B/C/S version and page 8 in the English version, you say -- could you please record -- can you please state that I am going on record as saying that Mr. Delic is not a member of the Presidency unless Mr. Petkovic is sitting next to him: "So let's reach a decision, either both of them or neither one. If we cannot vote on this now since military issues are not on the agenda, can we at least then discuss the issue?" End of quote. Mr. Akmadzic, can you please tell us what were you calling for at this meeting of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted -- what I wanted was that in accordance with the decision of the War Presidency that the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina consisted of the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council and since a representative of the army or representatives in the War Presidency become members, they should have been representatives of the Territorial Defence, but Territorial Defence was no more that either the chiefs of both component parts of the army should sit on the Presidency or neither, but I also indicated that because it was not on the agenda, rules of procedure of the Presidency must be adhered to. I wanted this to be debated and perhaps a decision could be postponed for some other time but until a decision is taken, Rasim Delic is not a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, please tell us whether the president of the Presidency ever tabled this topic, whether this was put on the agenda and did you decide on this issue whether those chiefs of staff would be members of the Presidency or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president was evasive about this. He asked for Rasim Delic to be a member of the Presidency until we took a different decision. I said no and that was the Presidency decision. He is not a member of the Presidency until we have a decision for him to become one, a joint decision or rather along with Mr. Petkovic or the chief of the HVO staff, whoever this happened to be. In any case, along with Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This was all going on in 1993. What about 1992? Were there any initiatives back in 1992 by the Croat members of the Presidency to, for example, set up some sort of a joint command for the two armies, the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On our part, there was several such initiatives. They were always voiced as part of the work of the Presidency and the government. There were initiatives within the HVO itself. There were even agreements and talks. In a way, and in a formal sense, there was not a joint command perhaps that was set up but there was an agreement on a joint command, however, this never really started operating until the Washington talks were over.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned the Washington Agreement, can you please go to my small, small, very small binder. This is 4D 1234. This is a document, it's a letter by Ambassador Sacirbey and Ambassador Nobilo to the Security Council. Attached to the letter is the Washington Agreement. Mr. Akmadzic, if you look at the copy that is in our language, you will see only a portion of the Washington Agreement as the framework on the BH federation. What I want to know at this point in time is this: Item 6 of the agreement, military agreement. We can have a look. Both parties have agreed to the establishment of a unified military command of the military of the federation. I skip the following paragraph and take it on: "Current command structures will remain in place. Forces of the sides will disengage from one another immediately ..." and then, "all foreign armed forces except those present with the agreement of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the authorisation of the UN Security Council will leave the territory of the federation." Sir, Mr. Akmadzic, you were involved in the creation of the Washington Agreement; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please help us with this to better understand item 6. This provision here, where it says that a joint military command would be set up, does this mean that this unified military command would be shared by the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The HVO and the BH army should have a unified command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It is also stated that the current command structures would remain until further notice. Does that this mean that even after the Washington agreement, the HVO would continue to operate with the same structure as before?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just the HVO. In both the political and the military sense, all the parties would continue to operate in this way until a different kind of agreement is reached, all the structures would be preserved and they would continue to work regardless these agreements until a different system was finally in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document now, this is also in my binder, this is 4D 8226. This is the law on the proclamation of the law on the defence of the BH federation. What I want to know about is Article 37. We have an English translation on this article. If you look at Article 37 of the BH federation law, we can find the following, 37 paragraph 2: "The federation army shall consist of units of the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council including the core level and the district level." Mr. Akmadzic, does this mean that much, like the BH army, the HVO continued to operate on its own until this law was adopted? And once this law was adopted, it became a component of the federation army same as the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. Based on what I know, the HVO is still a segment of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the HVO soldiers in terms of their rights, retirement, pensions, invalid status, shares and stocks. Was their status equal in every way to that of the BH army members? I'm talking about today in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think that it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. That concludes the first portion our examination and now I would like you to comment on the Jovo Divjak discussion? Before I embark on this, may I just say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, [as interpreted] the Chamber wonders what is the relevance for this case involving Mr. Divjak. Could you give us some additional information? What are you getting at?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With pleasure, Your Honours. Mr. Jovan Divjak was Mr. Sefer Halilovic's deputy. In November or December 1992, he was arrested under the suspicion that he had stoked up the clashes between the Croats and Muslims in Prozor on the 23rd and 24th of October 1993 [as interpreted]. This is an incident mentioned in our indictment as incriminating. I think it is essential for us to show you or to try to show you that within the top-most structures of the BH army, there was a top-level commander who was accused of inciting the Croats and the Muslims; and that resulted in a clash since the OTP was saying this was something triggered by Croats and wrapped up by Croats and that they were attacking Muslim civilians, what I'm trying to show you is that that was, in fact, not the case. We have an exceptional opportunity here and maybe this is our last opportunity to discuss this transcript and to discuss the part of the discussion at the Presidency about the arrest of Mr. Jovo Divjak whereas the witness, Mr. Akmadzic, said at this meeting that maybe it was as true as well the reason why Jovan Divjak was arrested because after -- my question to the witness, I want to show him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, would you please care to look at page 37, lines 21 and 23. Something must be wrong with the dates. You said he was not arrested in December 1992 for having committed misdeeds in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. The other year is 1992 as well. Everything that goes on in connection with Mr. Divjak has to do with the incident in Prozor in October 1992. The arrest, the discussion of his arrest and the statement that Mr. Jovo Divjak made and I believe we'll have a look at that as long as that is okay with the Chamber that has to do with late 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may proceed. We understand that this is in connection with Prozor. It was not obvious in the documents. This issue was not mentioned during the examination in chief led by Mr. Karnavas so the time you will spend on that issue will be taken out of the time of your examination in chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course it is for the Chamber to rule on. I just wish to point out that document was shown to the witness yesterday and this document in its entirety I assume will be admitted into evidence. I also believe that my cross-examination about any portion of that transcript must be considered as cross-examination; and as Mr. Karnavas himself said, these transcripts comprise a number of really important statements and observations. However, the Prlic Defence ran out of time, and they couldn't discuss each of these topics. However, the document was used in chief, and I think I should be granted time to examine on this in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I'm not sure that I've greeted the courtroom this afternoon so I'll do it now. Good afternoon, Your Honours, to all those in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, I just wanted to again to be consistent with the issues the Prosecution have been raising for some weeks now since the beginning of the Defence case, I believe. We just again want to say that we do not consider this -- what we've heard so far to be cross-examination. This is a direct examination of a friendly witness on these point and at all should be considered direct examination and there should not be any leading questions put. Secondly, Your Honours, as a second aspect of the concerns that we continue to raise. When Mr. Karnavas -- I'm not picking on Mr. Karnavas but any party when it was the Prosecution's case, it was the Prosecution, if it's now the Prlic case, eventually it will be the Stojic case, et cetera, we are required -- everyone is required to provide a 65 ter notice. This is a perfect example of a topic, the involvement of Mr. Divjak where the Prosecution has had no notice whatsoever, I mean none, zero, not a pair paragraph, not a word, not a jittle or jottle or whatever one might call it; so Your Honour we continue to believe this is a fundamental flaw in the process raising topics that the Prosecution has had absolutely no notice of. I mean Judge Prandler, absolutely no notice, never heard this before. So it's a flaw in the process, Your Honour when there's going to be additional direct examinations by other co-accused of a witness and they must -- and with the greatest respect to my good friend, Ms. Alaburic, she must have known just more than five minutes ago that she was going to do this, and I mean that with the greatest respect. I have I have been working on my cross-examination for days, not just now, although this is a new topic that I now have to deal with overnight perhaps but surely there must be some means for other co-accused examining a witness to provide some notice of what their examinations will be so that everyone can prepare. Part of the problem with the documentation, Your Honours, part of the frustration with the amount of documentation is because you have to prepare great volumes of material potentially that might potentially be used guessing -- trying to guess what might come up. And therefore, it puts everyone and particularly in this case the Prosecution in a position where we, given the lack of prior statement, given the lack of an adequate summary, we have to basically guess some weeks in advance based on the trial calendar when a witness is coming and guess what documents might be relevant; and the Chamber may or may not be concerned about that. It may have no sympathy for the Prosecution position at all, but I submit to the Chamber that it is not -- number one it's not fair to the Prosecution. Number two, it adds to the problem that we all combat with a number of documents and the preparation that's involved. It is all related.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard just for a couple of moments. First and foremost, this topic was indeed on our list because we had discussed it with the gentleman. We didn't get the chance to get to it because we ran out of time. Secondly, the -- if the Prosecutor had looked at the list of documents that we had submitted and these are presidential transcripts or other transcripts that were available to them, they would be able to see where Mr. Akmadzic's name is referenced and look at the documents. Thirdly, I -- I don't recall receiving any sympathy from the members of the Trial Chamber when we were doing our cross-examination. It is what it is. We got a list from the Prosecution when we were doing our cross-examination based on that list we read all the documents. We then did our own searches and from there, further searches, and we would come up with a list of documents and prepare our cross-examination accordingly. Let me remind the Trial Chamber in the United States in the federal system for instance, the defence does not get anything other than the statement of the accused, nothing from the witness, until after the witness testifies on direct examination which is -- this is true and you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's not true where I practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't see where the problem lies. It is incumbent on the Prosecutor to look at the documents that we've submitted, that we indicate we're going to put to the witness and from there on, it is for them to figure out where we're going. And if they are prepared and they should and they are, they know where we are going. Lastly, I want to remind the Trial Chamber that this gentleman did indeed testify in the -- and members of the Prosecution were fully aware of it and one of the Prosecutors, in fact, in this courtroom was engaged, in my understanding, in that particular case. So they had a transcript of this gentleman from a previous testimony, there was also a statement that was taken, I don't know whether they have it or not, but when you look at the transcript, it's obvious. I believe Mr. Scott was involved in that particular case, so I don't see where the drama lies and I think Ms. Alaburic and other Defence teams should be entitled to go into areas whether I omitted to do it because it's not part of my case or I'm trying to work within the time limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, you were, if I could respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What a waste of time but you may go on, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest respect, I don't think it's a waste of time. I think the -- my position happens to be and maybe I'm the only one in the courtroom who believes it, but my position happens to be that the international community, the victims in this case, and the Prosecution as a party is entitled to fair process. Now maybe I'm the only one who thinks that. I will mention to the Chamber, I will mention to the Chamber that in reference to the summary, the Rule 65 summary we received, there is no reference about anything about Mr. Divjak. We've raised this before. There are two long paragraphs that are extremely generic, so he didn't testify about in the Kordic case, it doesn't touch -- it's not in the summary and it's a fundamental point of notice, Your Honour, what is so difficult, what would be so unfair or so burdensome so oppressive to the Defence to provide the Prosecution some reasonable notice? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall consult my fellow Judges. I will give you the floor later on. First I'd like to consult my fellow Judges in order to see whether we will give Ms. Alaburic the possibility to put leading questions on not, whether it's within examination in chief or cross-examination, we'll see about that later. We'll first decide whether she should be authorised to put leading questions. What would you like to say, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it is a waste of time because of course motions, Your Honours are seized of a motion on -- very this exact point about the Prosecution's repeated insistence that cross-examination by other accused should be classed as examination in chief. That's a matter of judice at the moment, and it's continuous repetition and the, no doubt, very sincere and very strongly felt views of my learned friend do not get better in my respectful submission by mere repetition. To that extent, I do respectfully submit that Mr. President, and Your Honours are quite right that it is an unnecessary waste of time. In relation to the atmosphere of the courtroom, it's also -- Your Honours of course are very recently come into this case, but one of the reasons why I think sometimes the atmosphere degenerates is by unnecessary immotive language and it behoves no party to wear either the interests of justice or the interests of victims as if an -- and arrogate those interests themselves. The Defence don't wear on that I sleeve their passion or at least they shouldn't, and I do respectfully submit it doesn't do my learned friend, Mr. Scott, who's a very experienced and very fine Prosecutor and lawyer justice to continuously belabour that point. It doesn't advance the actual submissions that Your Honours have. Your Honour, the third point, of course, it's in your inherent powers to mold and craft rules of procedure that are intended to get to a more fair and expeditious conduct of a trial, but this is not a plenary. The rules are there and Rule 65 ter which my learned friend refers to simply doesn't refer to information that's put in cross-examination. When my learned friend was -- when my learned friend cross-examines, the convention is that prior to cross-examination he will give the documents he intends to put to confront a witness to the other party. That's what my learned friends have done. It's what all Defence counsel do, and I don't see that seeking to get a rule changed that the -- that Your Honours could do in plenary by the back door takes matters further. Your Honour, my learned friend Mr. Karnavas is quite right in relation to the United States practice of course Mr. Scott is a master of his own system. I'm not, I'm not from that system at all. But what is clear beyond paradventure is that in the United States of America, he would be in a far more disadvantaged position than he is before this international court; and he does the Judges of this court a great disservice to bleat on or continuously repeat that this is unfair because he does have access, he knows exactly who is going to be called whereas in the United States, he has no idea who is behind the door and who is the next witness. And, Your Honour, in the United States of America, in the United States of America, my learned friend can operate with far less information. American lawyers operate with far more -- far less information, and it cannot be said that a lawyer as skilled with the resources of the Prosecution as experienced as Mr. Scott suffers a huge diminution of his experience and his qualifications and his ability to deal with these witnesses simply by crossing the Atlantic. For those reasons, Your Honour, it's my submission that all of this has been an unnecessary waste of time and could have been prevented.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just two sentences before you start deliberating. I would like to stress that in this transcript, we now have at least five pages dealing with the arrest of Mr. Jovo Divjak, and I would also like to remind my learned friend Mr. Scott that Mr. Stojic's Defence Exhibit 2D 00263 was admitted into evidence a long time ago, and you have it in the binder relating to the examination of this witness and this document discusses the arrest of Mr. Divjak. We cross-examined Prosecution witnesses on this topic. So I will not be asking Mr. Akmadzic any other questions different from what we asked other witnesses. The only difference being that this witness was present at the meeting of the Presidency where this was discussed. He heard explanations proffered by Mr. Halilovic and I consider it to be my professional obligation to seek further explanations from this witness about issues that we discussed with Prosecution witnesses earlier on in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, one minute, one minute to respond. I watch the clock, and I promise it won't be more than one minute. First of all in response to Mr. Khan. My comments were measured the record will show I wasn't raising my voice and when I think the some of the theatrics that have gone on in this trial in the last two years, I think my comments were measured, calm, no one was wearing their emotions on their sleeve. It was a principal point, and a principal point that I continue to believe very much. Secondly, it's -- I'm not trying to take away counsel's opportunity to go into it but just give us notice. And the proposition for anyone to suggest there are thousands literally thousands of documents in this case and because a document is somewhere in the trial record that the Prosecution should guess and have to anticipate what is going to come up in an examination is simply a completely ridiculous proposition with the greatest respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we just say we support the Petkovic -- we support what Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Khan have said, but I would reassure Mr. Scott, there is certain hyperbolic language, maybe he is the only one in the courtroom that thinks that the Prosecution is entitled to a fair process -- I expect he'd have Mr. Bos with him at the very least.
