But, Your Honours, we all accept, we never submitted anything so ridiculous is that the Prosecution is not entitled to a fair process. What we do is we do disagree from time to time about what is needed for there to be a fair process, and that is what we are talking about; and as Mr. Khan has indicated, all these issues are in the pretty elaborate written submissions which are before Your Honours following a motion by the Prosecution. Now of course we could all invite Your Honours to give us the ruling as soon as you can manageably do it, and we're sure that you wish to do it but it doesn't add anything to have these oral submissions while we're waiting for that ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Praljak, you are on your feet. Why? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would like to ask a question to you, Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of question? Because my colleagues -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] It relates to the constant reiteration on the part of the Prosecution that we are responsible to the international community. Am I responsible to laws or to a political organisation which is termed the international community and which may involve all kinds of things. I would just this to be made clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Judges are going to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber has discussed the issue. First of all, regarding the intervention by Mr. Praljak. This is a Tribunal that renders justice. It is not the international community. Secondly, with regard to the application by Ms. Alaburic. The questions to be asked based on these two documents must be non-leading questions. Thirdly, the Trial Chamber points out that indeed the Prosecution, during the Prosecution case, had written statements; however, when it comes to the Defence case, we do not have prior statements, only documents are being introduced. In some cases, the Prosecution can legitimately believe that it is prejudiced. That is all we want to say. Ms. Alaburic, you can put your questions, however, I can't tell you whether you're going to have time or not. But put your questions in a general fashion without them being leading and that will be enough just as Judges do when they have their questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this transcript, and we should not be wasting any time -- don't go looking for it, I'll just make -- give a page reference for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. It's page 01806421 and this is in document 1D 2663. I think it is in the second binder provided by the Prlic Defence. So Mr. Akmadzic, we're talking about whether Mr. Divjak was arrested or not, Sefer Halilovic provides some explanations that really don't make it quite clear what happened and you say, let me quote from the page that I just referenced: "Are we sure about what the charges are against Mr. Divjak. Allegedly those charges do not stand." So your question is whether there were grounds for Mr. Divjak's arrest in light of the charges against him. Can you please explain to us what was this all about?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously we were talking about two elements in the Presidency. Some members of the Presidency were aware of the situation and others were not. The fact is that Mr. Divjak was arrested. It is also a fact that Mr. Halilovic claimed that this was not an arrest proper. He was brought into custody, something like that. Nobody says explicitly why Mr. Divjak was arrested and no explanation is given as to the circumstances, what actually happened. So my question was that he was probably charged with something that happened. Why would somebody arrest the deputy chief of -- general staff of the army just like that? And I sought information and the conclusion was that this would be discussed at this session before it ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please now look at document 2D 263. It's a report from commander Arif Pasalic to his superior Sefer Halilovic and in the first paragraph of this report, this is what it says: "On the 2nd of December, 1992 at 10.30 hours, the Neretvica brigade members in a building owned by Zejnil Delalic an arrest was made and the person was arrested was Jovo Divjak. The reason why he was arrested was the assumption that he was in collusion with the persons who committed a number of crimes in the territory of the municipality of Konjic or rather that Mr. Jovo Divjak participated in issuing orders that were aimed at causing a rift between the Croat and Muslim peoples on the ground, and I now will now skip the rest in my narrative. Mr. Akmadzic, could you please tell me does this tally with the information that you had at the time about the reasons for Mr. Jovo Divjak's arrest?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and this was not the explanation that was given at the Presidency meeting. I have just indicated that it is possible that some of the Presidency members such as Izetbegovic and Halilovic perhaps knew about that, but the rest of us we didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you now please look at 4D 427. Could we perhaps now see whether you received any further information about that? Did you learn that Mr. Jovo Divjak provided a statement regarding his arrest?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that, but I never did receive this statement in the written form.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 3, that's both in the English and the B/C/S version. Mr. Divjak says, as regards the Prozor case and the relations between Croats and Muslims or rather the BH army and the HVO: "I reject any suspicion that I fermented those conflicts. I will go as far as to say that I assisted on trying to calm the situation down, to get people to talk." So does this correspond to what you knew about Mr. Divjak giving such a statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that at that time, you did not receive any information as to why Mr. Divjak was actually arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received any information to that effect at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my cross-examination. Mr. Akmadzic, thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me come back to Ms. Nozica, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you. While the binders are being distributed in the courtroom, I would like to say good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom including the witness, and I would like to say that I will be -- that I will have more cross-examination for this witness. I was given some time both by the Defence of Mr. Coric and the Defence of Mr. Pusic, and I want to be certain that if any of this time is subtracted from the time allotted to me for the cross-examination, that that be only my time not the time of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, I must discuss this with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, we discussed this issue because at one point in time, you said that the others had given you some time. The Trial Chamber had pondered this issue and had decided not to allow time being given by other teams; however, on a case-by-case basis, the Trial Chamber may give extra times. We said there would be three hours by the Defence teams altogether now if you are the only one to intervene with Ms. Alaburic if we divide three hours by five you would have had 36 minutes for your own time. But we have time available and, of course, we shall authorise you to do more than 36 minutes but not from the time given by Mr. Pusic or Mr. Coric. Did you understand?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I understand Your Honour but I find this highly confusing and I simply have to state this on the record. The last time Ms. Alaburic spoke up and said that all of the Defence teams had a total of 15 minutes which divided by 5 would amount to 5 minutes and -- 3 minutes, I don't remember exactly. Judge Trechsel said entire defence all the Defence teams got 15 minutes. How you use it is entirely up to you. This is just what we did today. We sat down together and we reached an agreement. As far as I know, no one save for Ms. Alaburic and myself will be crossing this witness simply because it's a fair thing to do, I talked to my colleagues, I found out that they would not be cross-examining this witness and I informed the Chamber. Therefore, this time is now mine based on what Judge Trechsel said the last time around, I organised my cross-examination. It will be longer than 36 minutes, that's for sure. I hope to receive more instructions now from the Chamber. I have to be allowed to complete my cross-examination because if 36 or 40 minutes is all I'm getting, I will have to pare back, I will have to cut down on what I was planning for originally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're confused, whether we're similarly confused or confused in a different way, I don't know. Your Honour, what's happening now seems to us not to accord with the guidelines which Your Honours issued on the 24th of April, 2008. I'm talking about the decisions adopting guidelines for the presentation of Defence evidence because in paragraph 15, it says and this is about four or five lines from the bottom, "Unless the Chamber decides otherwise the teams shall agree among themselves on the allocation of time and inform of Chamber of this in advance." It seems to contemplate exactly that and certainly we do adopt and support what Ms. Nozica has said. It seems to have followed from everything that Your Honours had previously said in the course of what's so far been Mr. Karnavas's case that that was the system. Your Honours, again we've got some -- all sorts of written material before the courts at the moment on the question of these guidelines, but if a new issue has arisen, then we all need to have a full opportunity of addressing it fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to look into this again, of course without prejudice to anybody. We decided that the Defence would have three hours for cross-examination. You can use, Ms. Nozica and Ms. Alaburic the three hours allocated.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Your Honours. At the outset there was one thing that I wished to say. I will be dealing with several topics. I believe that these topics have been raised in chief. I believe this is indeed cross-examination that I'm about to embark on. There is one topic that wasn't raised. It has to do with two documents, 2D 544 and 2D 705. It's about the contact between this witness and the HVO's health department in 1993. I will underline this as soon as I broach this subject. Before I start, I want to say that I ordered my documents in these binders in the order in which I will be examining this witness. I knew ahead of time what Judge Trechsel would be after and I wanted to make his job as easy as possible. In addition to this, I have Defence 1D documents in my binder, therefore you will not be needing any other binders. I know about -- I know all about the weight of Defence 1D's shoulders, and it will probably be just as difficult for me to order my binders in the right way for the convenience of the Chamber but in this situation, it was somewhat easier for me to be facing fewer exhibits, far fewer exhibits, I should say than my learned friend, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, again, witness. For the record, after all we've met before, haven't we; but my name is Senka Nozica, and I represent with my colleague Mr. Stojic. I would start with a document just to avoid any misunderstandings, this was in Mr. Karnavas's binder. This is 1D 2067. You've got my binder in front of you, sir. This is the statement of the members of the HV Presidency, your statement of the 21st of April, 1993. During this trial, we have been using this statement. There was a witness here whose name I'm not allowed to mention. In the further course of my cross examination I will only be focussing on the first portion of this statement. The document says at the meeting of the Presidency members, the prime minister and the members of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croat ones held yesterday in Mostar in connection with the acts of aggression carried out by the Muslim forces against the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina a statement was adopted that we hereby publish in it's entirety. Mr. Akmadzic, my question would be at the time what sort of information was available to you, prior to the 21st of April, prior to this statement being made public about the military activities of the BH army? Let's try to limit this to Central Bosnia in terms of geography?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this before, but I'd like to repeat this. We're talking about April 1993 and this was one of the most difficult months as far as the situation in Central Bosnia was concerned, one of the worst months if you like. The BH army as one of the component parts of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina is attacking another component arm of the army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as the population of Central Bosnia. The BH Presidency, a body that we had by this time addressed both directly and indirectly was doing nothing about this. At a meeting that we held, we stated that we were effectively powerless to stop the clashes. We made a public declaration, a statement for the benefit of both the domestic and international public to the effect that we were facing a very difficult situation and that our people were under attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, I would like to ask you a very specific question: Did you at any point in time know anything at the time you were making this statement about the army attacks on Zenica and Travnik, that general area in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not aware of the attack on Zenica. We were aware of an attack that was launched from Zenica on Travnik specifically, on Bugojno, on Novi Travnik. Actually, for the most part, the areas coming under attack were areas where there were very important military factories in Bosnia and Herzegovina and armament factories.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, when I said on Zenica, I meant attacks on the HVO in Zenica but your intervention was perfectly appropriate. But can you explain this when you say attacks on areas that held the most important military factories in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was that the conclusion at the time or had you already caught wind of the possibility that there might be some activity along these lines in precisely these areas?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had caught hints that something like this might happen. I would like to tell the Chamber that Central Bosnia is the very heart of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We talked in answer to different question about the kingdom of Bosnia as it used to be. It was precisely in Central Bosnia, in Vares, that the king had his thrown, his seat. It is there that the coat of arms of the kingdom of Bosnia are still kept or at least I hope so. It is precisely in Central Bosnia as it is that in Travnik, we have a clothing factory for the military. In Novi Travnik and Bugojno, we have factories that produce weapons for the military. In Konjic, there is another such factory that produces weapons for the military. When Jajce fell, the Muslims started moving towards Central Bosnia as refugees. There was a disbalance. Now, this is something that I addressed with Mr. Izetbegovic. He said we'll deal with this disbalance or this disharmony in terms of population movement. However, it was quite obvious to me that he was either unable or unwilling to deal with this. We knew about the impending danger looming over Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May I ask you or perhaps remind you because I believe this is something that you actually know. You spoke about all these towns. You spoke about a number of towns with military production facilities. You omitted Vitez, was Vitez not another such town?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vitez was equally important in this context. This was an explosive factory in Vitez and explosives were needed in order to be able to use all these weapons being produced. But we're talking about the aggression being carried out by the BH army at this period of time. In my assessment, and that may be the reason for this omission, Vitez was not at risk to the same extent. It would be very much at risk but that wasn't until a little later, regardless of the fact that there were attacks against Vitez as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, you spoke about this disbalance, how the balance, the population balance was tipped when a large number of Muslims arrived in Central Bosnia and then you spoke about these military factories producing weapons in Central Bosnia. Is my understanding correct, I think you were saying something along the lines that there were expectations that the BH army would be attacking HVO units in these areas. Is my conclusion accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were perfectly aware of the danger, and we warned the Presidency that certain steps should be taken. I talked to Mr. Izetbegovic, and I talked to him about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me now take you through a couple of documents addressing the military situation in Central Bosnia, specifically Zenica and Kakanj areas which is something that you addressed already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, if you want to move on to another document, I have a question on this one dealing with a topic you did not tackle. Dealing with item or paragraph number 3, would you mind looking at it? In a very clear manner, you speak about the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic usurped his Presidency since you said that his mandate had expired on the 20th December, 1992 and therefore he usurped his function and this is something you said on the 21st of April, 1993. Upon reading this, I have the following question: The Croat members in the Presidency were of the view that the Presidency operated illegally for a legal ground that you expanded upon but how is it then that you and your fellow Croats, possibly also the Serbs, failed then to tell the international community, because there were a lot of negotiations going on, why did you not say that given that situation, you would withdraw for all negotiations and that the international community had to deal with it only with the usurpers? Why did you not take up this position because then maybe there would have been a problem vis-a-vis the negotiators who would have had only one side facing them and not the three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we informed the international community about this. We informed the co-chairmen who to us represented the international community. We know the international community is a generic notion, it is not a body in the proper sense, it is not a legal entity. For us during the negotiations, the international community meant the UN and the western European Union. We never went beyond that framework because the co-chairmen were appointed at the London Conference and the scope of that conference was even broader than what I have now been referring to. There is one thing that I would like to share with the Chamber. It wasn't just about us but the difficulties of the Croats in particular were great. The international community, in a manner of speaking, on the one hand had to deal with the Presidency, it had no choice but to deal with the Presidency. On the other hand, there were the three clashing parties which it had no choice but to deal with either. None of us ever questioned the fact that Alija Izetbegovic was a legitimate member of the BH Presidency. None of us ever questioned the fact that he was representing the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina. All we wished to underline was the fact that the BH Presidency had to operate in keeping with its own rules of procedure, the rules of procedure under which it was established, in keeping with the constitution and the laws of the country. The Presidency had to see us or treat us as a constituent people. We had no insight into any decisions that were being taken, many of them at the same time, actually. It wasn't just the Presidency. We had no access to many of the decisions or their implementation taken by the Presidency itself. This is the background to our reaction. We started with this letter, it's actually not a letter, it's more of a declaration. We started with this and at a later stage we realised that we had not succeeded in achieving what we believed was necessary. As I said yesterday, we froze all of our activities in the Presidency and the government in a bid to use any legal avenues available to us in order to get the Muslims to at least start implementing such decisions as had been adopted, and we wanted to get them to cooperate in terms of the talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at document 2D 00472, that's the next document in line. For the transcript, I would like to say that this is an exhibit. It's an order for an attack, it's a BH army document from the 7th Muslim Brigade, the 2nd Zenica Battalion command, the date is the 17th of April and in this order for attack, in paragraph 1, it says, on the axis of the attack of the battalion, the defence is amounted by the enemy strength such and such in order to defend the town of Zenica et cetera and the suburbs. Mr. Akmadzic, could you please confirm that this was the information that you had about the attacks on the HVO, let me be quite specific, in Zenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely and if I may, to clarify to the Trial Chamber this issue, the Croatian Defence Council existed in areas where Croats were in the minority. One of the towns where the Croatian Defence Council existed is Zenica, the town that we have here, but there was the Croatian Defence Council in Sarajevo, the town where I lived. So the Croatian Defence Council and all the structures of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as it was at the time existed throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina regardless of the ethnic composition of the population. In this specific case that I have in front of me now, this is an attack on the HVO mounted by a much larger force, a superior force, a larger segment of the armed forces, the attacking a weaker segment of the armed forces. We had been receiving complaints from Zenica. We couldn't prevent those attacks. It is my assessment that the reason why we couldn't stop those attacks was because the extremists were out in force in the town of Zenica at this time that we're now discussing other forces from abroad, either organised or on an individual basis were joining the BH army, now I'm talking primarily about the Mujahedin. At this time, within the framework of the BH army or perhaps I should say outside of the framework of the BH army, there were other forces operating such as for instance the MOS, the Muslim armed forces, and we couldn't negotiate with them, we couldn't cooperate with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, you mentioned something that goes beyond the topic that I wanted to discuss but it would be pertinent. Could you please explain to the Judges outside the territory of the HZ HB, there were HVO units. You mentioned Sarajevo, you said that throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were such units?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes in Tuzla, in Bihac, in the Posavina area, in Zenica, in Vares in Kakanj. I'm not talking about locations where the population was mixed and where Muslims were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you tell us the HVO units in Sarajevo and in other places, who did they fight against and who did they fight side-by-side with?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, at least at the beginning, there were no conflicts between the BH army and the HVO. There was full cooperation, and they fought side-by-side against the aggressor as this aggressor was defined.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't like that up until the very end, but I don't want to go into this topic, but this was not the case up until the very end. There was a conflict and there was forcible resubordination to the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no conflicts in the real sense of the word. There was some misunderstandings. The BH Presidency as the supreme commander attached or rather joined the brigade of the HVO that existed in Sarajevo to the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, we will call a witness that will explain how the HVO functioned throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it's an important topic. But let us know go back to the issue of Zenica. Could you please look at document 2D 101. It's the next document in the binder. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica, before we leave this one. In the first paragraph Witness, it is stated the reasons for the order, the background, "Based on recent development of the events, situation and behaviour of HVO troops and with aim to prevent surprise ..." Do you have any information, can you inform the Chamber of what was referred to by the behaviour of HVO troops. You may not know what they referred to, and I completely accept that; but I would like to give you the opportunity to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that this preamble when it mentions the developments, what it mentions the negotiations, political negotiations that were conducting at the time, the political situation in the country. I don't know anything about the conduct or behaviour of the HVO units, but I can assume that there were some problems in cooperation although the HVO did propose that joint command be set up. So I couldn't really say what is meant when the words "the behaviour of the HVO units" is mentioned and they are not talking about the HVO as a whole but only about the unit that they are in contact with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But I think that we will be able to clear this up with the next document, that's 2D 101.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report on the organisation of the HVO in Zenica and the events that preceded its neutralization in the Zenica municipality area. This is a report that was sent by Vinko Baresic, the commander of the Zenica Brigade of the HVO. Mr. Akmadzic, let me put some parts of this report to you. The date is the 23rd of April 1993 so it includes the events of the 17th and the 18th of April. And since you have already seen this -- these documents, I would just like to point some elements to you. In the introduction, the commander of the Zenica Brigade of the HVO indicates that he was for all intents and purposes a member of the BH army in Zenica, that in June 1992, he was transferred to the HVO and that the situation was fine until November 1992 as regards the relations between the HVO and the BH army; and that is when the command of the 3rd Corps of the BH army was set up, headquartered in Zenica. The commander goes on to say that this is when the problems began cropping up. He says that the information service of the 3rd Corps usurped all the public media with a plan that they had and the fierce campaign stating that the BH army was the only force fighting for the sovereign unified indivisible Bosnia and Herzegovina. At page 2 of this document, that's in the Croatian version, and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, this is page 0062 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction 61.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it says here the pressure in Zenica is increasing. I think the answer in this question one asked by Judge Trechsel, there was sporadic killings and abductions where people were being taken away and nobody knows where we are. When we protest about this to the civilian authorities and the BH army, we get the same reply, that is, they have nothing to do with that; and they will do everything if those acts were committed by members of the BH army to investigate this, but they never wanted to admit that they were responsible or to take the blame and they never identified the perpetrators. The indications that we received in the best scenario cases were that those were individuals who were not under their control and that they distanced themselves from those individuals and their media would inform the public that those -- that this was, in fact, lack of discipline on the part of the HVO fighters who would have to be placed under the control of the official and regular army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is the BH army. The text goes on to say that the HVO in Zenica did have information that the situation was in fact the exact opposite. It was a serious situation. The public was being prepared for the final showdown with the HVO in Zenica, the command of the 7th Muslim Brigade was set up in Zenica; and the document goes on to say that this command was set up to include for the most part foreign volunteers of the Mujahedin who drove around Zenica or ran around the town bearing their religious banners and singing songs in a language that one could or could not understand in a show of force and members of those units did all the dirty work in Central Bosnia for the most part in the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, was this the information that you had when you talked about the Mujahedin and when you talked about the preparations for this pressure designed to defeat the HVO in this area militarily?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm concerned that we're going to spend some three hours with five minute questions and then asking if the witness can say anything about it. That was a five-minute question. I looked at the transcript. And I think we have to break it down and look at the witness's knowledge for this. How does he know about it? Does he -- has he ever seen this document before? Does he actually know anything about it ought all? I mean we seem to be just reading documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It hasn't escaped me. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want with this witness -- well, this document was tendered and was not admitted and now I want to go through all the documents that are relevant for the Defence and find out whether the witness has any knowledge of those events and those documents because that will make our job easier. There is a lot of relevant details in this document I would like to go through it as fast as possible, and what I just quoted from this document confirms what the witness had already said. I would just like the witness to give us a brief answer. I would like to now go through two more details that are contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to note for the benefit of the Trial Chamber that I was a prime minister in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that I did not -- I do not like to get any suggestions as to what I should say, and I will just present my own views to the Trial Chamber the way I see things. I have already said and I would like to say this again to the Trial Chamber that the Croatian Defence Council and the BH army were partners, and they cooperated well over a certain period of time. As I have already said, and this was the view shared by us in the Presidency, the relations got worse because of the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina and the overall situation. When we're talking about this document, I don't know what individuals were in the HVO or in the BH army ranks were doing. I know that it was a firm agreement that we all reached that we should defend Bosnia and Herzegovina. In answer to another question, I said that it appears to me that there were extremists in the BH army ranks in Zenica and that regardless of all the agreements, one should never overlook the individuals who are involved and the people who are in charge of some units. Throughout the war we had huge problems with Zenica. The Croatian Defence Council in Zenica was just a small element of the joint armed forces. They were under pressure as this report shows, they were under pressure both from paramilitary formations. I don't know if anyone has told the Trial Chamber, if not, I would like to be the one to tell you this that the presence of foreign organised groups or individuals mostly in Central Bosnia led to great difficulties that continued on into the post-war period because without our knowledge and without our approval, many people were granted citizenship and this caused a lot of problems and laws had to be changed because of that. Then we faced the problem how can one -- how can one strip them of the citizenship that was granted to them and the international community had to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, well, you said this in answer to the Prosecution but you are spending my time. I don't want you to be under pressure but you saw that my time is limited. I think that we started an hour and a half ago, but I would just like Your Honours to tell me when there should be a break but perhaps if we could just complete this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we could have a break at half past 5.00 if that suits you. It's up to you. I'm entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, Your Honour, but the last break was a little earlier on. I thought now was the right time. I might as well press on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, you tell us that you've seen the document. Let me draw your attention to paragraph 3 in the Croatian version. I am -- I won't be reading it. It's 0063 in the English paragraph 2. The next paragraph after that, says the attack on the Zenica HVO started on the 18th of April at 05 hours, the next page claims that at about 1800 hours the Muslim forces took Zmajevac, this is very important, and the second to last page in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S claims that at the time, the reports were written on the 23rd of April, 1993 in Zenica there were no more HVO units remaining, members of the civilian authorities were under house arrest, most of the soldiers were in prisons apart from the HVO seals, everything else was in the hands of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could Ms. Nozica's microphones please be switched on and all the other microphones be switched off as she speaks. The interpreters cannot hear her properly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it is very difficult for me to address each of these elements simply because I wasn't there. However, based on the news that we got it was exactly like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we please now look at another document in reference to Zenica, briefly it's the next document 2D 00473. This is yet another order to launch another attack. Please tell me when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Indeed. This is an order to the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade as far as I can see, the 7th Muslim Brigade. It's just as we saw in that previous document, isn't it? With Zmajevac was taken. I would like to draw your attention to two salient details in this document if you look at paragraph 1 this is the second to last one not the last there is an attack on Zmajevac facility then if you go to paragraph 3, the last line, "Readiness for attack at 0500 hours on the 18th of April." This is entirely consistent with the report that we looked at. The Vinko Baresic report the commander of the HVO brigade. Is it consistent with your information at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's perfectly consistent with my information at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now for another document a very interesting one this is 2D 01405, this is a BH army document specifically the 3rd Corps. It bears the same date as the previous document, the 17th of April. The latter half of the document reads, the Bosnian Archbishop Monseigneur Vinko Puljic will be visiting the Zenica area over the next few days. Now the commander of the 3rd corps under Hadzihasanovic, if you go to paragraph 2 which is the following order, as part of this visit and generally speaking, any arrests of Croats shall be banned. No buildings or facilities shall be set fire to and no persons shall be mistreated. Mr. Akmadzic, the document speaks for itself doesn't it. It says as part of this visit but also generally speaking. Did you know anything about any further arrests, about the arrests continuing, the burnings continuing or the lootings continuing in Zenica continuing in the Zenica area?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I knew about that, but one must say that it is perfectly normal to put a stop to something like this during this visit by Cardinal Vinko Puljic given that Cardinal Vinko Puljic was held in very high esteem both as a religious figure and as a citizen, a human being, if you like. It was certainly not their intention to allow him to see anything like that going on or indeed as a result to make anything like that public.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will be showing you some things later on during my cross-examination. We will be looking at army documents and we will see what exactly was going on, but let us try to wrap this topic about the attack on Central Bosnia at the time. I'm talking about the 17th of April. Just for the benefit of the transcript. And this ties in with your statement as you said. Fine. This ties in with your statement on the 21st of April, the last document. This is 2D 01404, this is another order by the 3rd corps command. That reads one carry out reconnaissance along the Travnik-Vijenica-Stojkovici Axis the objective being to take that axis particularly the HVO storage facilities there. Is this consistent with what you were telling us about the plan and the attack in April 1993, the attack against the HVO and against Travnik? As we see it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes but this was happening, and I think I talked about this before. This is just a detail, a small thing in the general framework of all the attacks going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for this answer. We'll go on about this but we care about all these details because these details we can use as a later stage to put together the overall puzzle?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, maybe this would be a good time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm again going to object to this manner of proceeding, and I ask the Chamber to look at counsel's statements just now. All these details will be helpful we'll be using those in the future. The witness hasn't gone through and confirmed all these details, document are being put in front of this witness. We don't know if he's ever seen them before today or not and there's some pretense that he's confirming everything in the documents about any knowledge about any indication of the foundation for that, which facts he's affirming, which ones he don't; and on several occasions, the witness to his credit, I want to be fair about this, to his credit has said "I really don't know about that." But we just showing him more documents. The Chamber cannot go away with this evidence with all due respect in our submission and has any idea what the witness has either confirmed or not confirmed every detail in a multi-paged document cannot be done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understood properly but I may be wrong, the Defence has just shown you a series of military documents from the 3rd Corps. These documents establish that there was a large-scale operation in April launched by the 3rd Corps and it can be seen that the HVO members were arrested for instance in Zenica, Mr. Totic was also taken prisoner. I was under the impression that you were asked firstly whether you were aware of all this and whether the situation matched what you said during examination in chief as to actions by ABiH troops encouraged by Izetbegovic. Did I understand properly or not because the Prosecutor is telling us that all these documents are not known to you so please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I confirm these documents as such. My observation was about some of the details. There were many more elements which up to now have not been mentioned. There were other orders, there were other attacks in other towns as well. As far as I can tell, this is all about Zenica and Zenica's surroundings, however there were attacks being launched elsewhere as well. There's another thing that I would like to add. I don't know, maybe this wasn't Izetbegovic's order but it was certainly parted of his policy. And maybe there was an order in terms of this being the supreme command. He himself was not there in the area, and he couldn't issue any orders there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. Mr. Scott needn't worry we have the transcript, we can see clearly what the witness confirmed and what he denied. I think I built up a foundation for this. I asked him what he knew about what was going on in Central Bosnia. He said he was familiar and then he went on to describe what was going on and then I started using these documents but I think the transcript is there for everybody to see exactly what is going on and then the transcript will show the Trial Chamber exactly what the witness said, what he confirmed and what he denied. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. To begin with, I would like to apologise to all of our interpreters and particularly to the French booth because I was cautioned. They say I was speaking too fast towards the end. I will try to slow down now to ensure a quality interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, so far we've been talking about April 1993. I would like to move on to June 1993. Can you please look at 1D [as interpreted] 01406. I will show you portions of this document and after that my questions will be about the relations between the BH army and the Presidency, about the negotiations that were in progress at the time. This is a proclamation, a letter by the 3rd Corps Command, the date is the 9th of June. The second paragraph of this document reads, "The last talks between powerful players in Europe and the world were dictating the terms that we were to live with on our doorstep." This is 2D 1406. There appears to be an error in the transcript. The 3rd Corps released this declaration. We must face the truth, it reads, "We are left to our own devices. We have to turn to our own people." It calls on the citizens to unite and use everything that they had to defend the sovereignty, independence, integrity of the freedom of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a public call on the citizens. It is about gathering any weapons that the citizens had in their possession, the deadline given here is the 30th of June, and it also talks about the sanctions that will be imposed unless this is done. They are talking about the area under the command of the 3rd Corps. Mr. Akmadzic, this is something that we have discussed here and this is something that you raised in chief. At the time, negotiations were in progress. On the 18th of May, the Medjugorje Agreement was reached. Likewise you were shown a letter by Mr. Prlic dated December 1992. This is document 1D 01945. In this letter, Mr. Prlic talks about certain actions taken by Mr. Halilovic that were contrary to what had been agreed on the political level. My question is this: Is there anything you can tell us about how the BH army acted throughout these negotiations surrounding the Vance-Owen Plan, the negotiations that were referred to at the time. Is it true that they were adamant that the military operations should go ahead? And can you please explain the one thing that you said? Mr. Izetbegovic apparently told you in relation to his third term of office that he was willing to step down but the army, he said, wouldn't allow him. Can you tell us more about the BH army as a factor in those negotiations. Can you tell us about its power which apparently was a significant factor affecting the failure to accept the Vance-Owen Plan which is what was being discussed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, you referred to Mr. Sefer Halilovic. At one point in time, he clashed with Mr. Izetbegovic. Another thing that I wish to point out is this: At Presidency meetings, he would sometimes take the floor and say the army wants this, the army wants that. About this proclamation, he would probably have labelled it a pamphlet, and no more than that. But it was the same situation as I had previously faced in Sarajevo. They broke into my garage, they prowled around my house, they were looking for something that they could take from you. They were seizing your vehicles. None of this with any sort of prior approval from the Supreme Command. Along these lines, I could say that the BH army, regardless of the political circumstances in the Presidency itself harboured some views that were more extreme.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But if we tried to establish a link between this and Mr. Izetbegovic's statement that he would not have accepted the third term of office, that was not envisaged in the rules of procedure but that the army did not allow him to step down, would that mean that he in fact complied with the positions taken by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection. It sounds like a leading question to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just give a technical information. Witness, now in contrast to what happened most of the previous days, you are questioned in your own language and you have the natural tendency immediately to answer when you've understood the question. Please bear in mind that we understand the question considerably later because we wait for the interpretation and have a pause before you start speaking. Otherwise it becomes too difficult for the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this caution.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour but when Mr. Scott rose to his feet, I tried to rephrase my question but this is cross-examination, so I don't know why this objection was raised about the leading nature of the question. But let me rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic's statement that he would have stepped down had it not been for the army that did not allow him to do so, what was the relationship between the army and Mr. Izetbegovic then? Could you please answer that question? Because the army is in fact a political factor here. Could you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I started giving my answer, and my answer will be the same. I did not ask Mr. Izetbegovic what it meant. I did not ask him, and I cannot confirm that he was under any pressure from the army. But I can assume that in a way, the army leadership primarily Mr. Halilovic did tell him, President, do not let this post of the president out your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question raised by Ms. Nozica is most interesting because this is one of the first times that we seem to deal with this topic, namely that apparently between Izetbegovic and the army as represented by Halilovic, there would seem to be some kind of dissent. And when I heard the question, I sort of put myself back in January 1993 in Geneva when there were talks and discussions and unless I'm mistaken, I believe that Mr. Halilovic and Petkovic took part in talks with the international community. Could it be that Mr. Halilovic, when he was in Geneva, signed documents, took part in international negotiations, had not been given a clear and precise mandate from Mr. Izetbegovic so that in his back or in a parallel way or contrary would have his own game, could it be that whilst I remind -- recall that you were at some point in time prime minister so I suppose as such you had a word to say in some aspects related to defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When we're dealing with this time after the 20th of December, 1992 when the term of office expired for President Izetbegovic, at that time, the relationship between the president and General Halilovic and indeed the relationship between the Presidency and General Halilovic was not controversial. It became a problem later on in the course of the war and this is something that he spoke about, something that he speaks about now. In January 1993 in Geneva, General Halilovic negotiated and signed agreements with the approval of the president because the president never challenged this in any way and never made any indications to that effect. It is my personal opinion that when we're talking about the president's term of office, this was not any pressure from the army properly speaking, it was a proposal, a request, perhaps, that Mr. Izetbegovic blow up a little bit as he explained to me why he wanted to remain in that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So if we take what you said now as our starting point, this may have been just an attempt of Mr. Izetbegovic to justify himself. But let us move on to the events in Central Bosnia. I said at the beginning of this topic that we are talking about the beginning of June. You were asked questions by Mr. Karnavas, negotiations are ongoing in Geneva, an agreement was signed in Medjugorje on the 18th of May, and some modalities are being sought for the internal structuring the Bosnia and Herzegovina; and regardless of that, is it your knowledge that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina continued its attacks in this period, it continued attacking Vitez, Travnik and other areas in Central Bosnia and how does this fit in with this whole situation where on the one hand they are negotiating and on the other hand they are pursuing military activities attacking certain towns?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to stress here that the months of June and July were very tense months in terms of what we were doing at the time. The Vance-Owen Plan was not accepted. It was not being implemented. The BH Presidency met in the country and abroad. There is a great deal of discord among us. We were not in agreement about all of the issues pertaining to the future of our country and the structuring of our country, and I can only assume that this state of affairs was reflected on the armed forces too, it had an impact on them too, and the situation was very serious as it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question was: Do you have any information about attacks launched by the BH army in early, let's say, early June in the areas that I indicated, the Lasva Valley, Travnik and so on. Did you have any information about that and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we now please turn to document ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. You didn't quite answer the very interesting question by Ms. Nozica. You did answer, however -- I'm not quite satisfied with your answer. I'm going to tell you why. She told you that in June there were military actions in Vitez, in Travnik, and in Central Bosnia, and Ms. Nozica asked you how such military actions could take place whilst there were peace negotiations going on. It is a very well-put question indeed and everybody is waiting for your answer because there seems to be a contradiction, does there not? Everybody negotiating for peace, everybody is gathering for that purpose and applauding the effort and at the same time, there are military conflicts. You were one of the main players. Therefore, it would be interesting to know your view, to try and understand -- I mean -- because we were not there at the time, and we are trying to understand how there could be at the same time negotiations and an offensive in Central Bosnia because that cannot be denied, there was an offensive by the ABiH that is -- that went on into July, nearly until November. Can you answer? If you can't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until November -- I can give you a broader answer. When we are talking about this time period, Your Honours, I said that in my opinion, this discord and tension in the BH Presidency as the Supreme Commander had an impact on the BH army ranks where there was also tension. The uncertain outcome of the political negotiations because at this time, we didn't have the Vance-Owen Plan and the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan was not yet being drafted and this conflict was put in motion so that whoever takes more territory will have an advantage in the negotiations. I think that this is the key element. How to capture as much territory as possible in order to have stronger arguments. So it's the argument of force instead of the force of argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you have now answered. So you tried to get more, capture more territory to be in a better position at the negotiating table. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question, a very brief one. Given the situation, the Croats who globally were in agreement with the plan that was being created, the Vance-Owen Plan and later on, since you were on that track, at your level, why did you not speak to the international community to say: We agree with you 100 per cent but stop the others because they are the problem. Was anything done in that direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said this myself on a number of occasions, particularly when it came to the Vance-Owen Plan. Lord Owen himself replied saying: Mile, I'll say in this English. [In English] The Vance-Owen Plan is dead. [Interpretation] Yes. In this sense, and in negotiations that followed about other plans, we accepted everything because 17.5 per cent of the population, regardless of the equal status accorded to this population in the negotiations, is too little to try and persuade the 80 per cent of the population to look at things our way. In addition to the Croat-Muslim relations there was always the third partying, the aggressor party as we called it that had a huge territory under its control, the control of its armed forces -- I'm not going to go into figures now but I think at one point it was 70 per cent of the territory and in these international negotiations we referred to this situation as the fait accomplis. This was the strongest argument in the negotiations, unfortunately, or at least that's how it seemed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just really brief and the answer too. Could you date the moment when Lord Owen told you that the Vance-Owen Plan was dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I can't give you the date, but I think it was this time period that we're talking about. I think it was in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us go back to June and I think that we did lay a foundation for this series of questions about military developments so let us look very briefly at some military documents. The next document is 2D 1407. Could you please just tell me when you found it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well this is a document signed by Tihomir Blaskic. The date is the 9th of June, 1993 so it's the same date, the date when the 3rd Corps issued the proclamation. Very briefly I would like to point your attention to the first part, the Muslim forces and the Mujahedin have carried out an open aggression against the Croat areas in the Lasva region. In this attack, a brigade and some local Mujahedin units were Travnik and Rostovo and elements from the 7th Brigade are taking part. This MOS and Mujahedin attack destroyed and expelled the Croats from the Travnik municipality, but they were not happy with that, they launched a fierce attack on -- in the direction of Zenica, on Guca Gora, and 39 Croat villages were emptied out, thousands of Croats, because of the serious situation that the Travnik Brigade faces and in order to protect the lives of civilians, the women and children, we had to evacuate the Croatian civilians. Mr. Akmadzic, in this period, quite a few Croats left this area. Could you please tell me, to your knowledge, was this the result of military operations such as this one launched in June and July as specified yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain how my testimony will evolve from here. Am I to address just this period in time or also what happened later? Regardless, let me say that Central Bosnia, the Bosna River Valley, the Lasva Valley and the Vrbas Valley meant this: Whoever held sway over Central Bosnia which, as I said before is Bosnia's very heart, and nearby there is a stone with the inscription that says the centre of Yugoslavia and militarily, politically and strategically speaking, this was a very important place. For this reason, the focus of the BH army and any units attached to it, and also because of the factories that I mentioned, the Muslim side wanted to take control of this. We've been mentioning some towns, but we have not yet mentioned Fojnica, Kakanj or Vares which saw a lot of the population leave. In Fojnica, there is a monastery which is to all practical intents the keeper of the memory of the Bosnia -- of olden times two friars were killed there, friars at this time and friars in times long gone had a good relationship with both the state and the Muslim side. What I see, what I'm looking at causes me no surprise because these are the holiest things to all Croats in Bosnia, churches and monasteries. What the Croats hold dearest. These were virtually destroyed. I can't vouch for this because I didn't go there myself, I didn't see this for myself, but one thing I do know is that at various points they all came under attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, you said the Croat population moved. I remember that. But we need to be more specific about that. When you say the population moved, what does that mean in the context of the times and then can we briefly look at 2D 00902. I suppose you've got that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is roughly the same time, the 11th June 1993. This is a public statement again signed by Mr. Blaskic and it reads: "Today, there is a disaster in progress among the peoples of Central Bosnia, Croat towns and villages. Over 30.000 refugees and homeless persons are looking for refuge in Novi Travnik, Vitez and Busovaca in a bid to escape the soulless Muslim fighters. The Croats are henned in, waiting to be shot. The White Lilies are shelling and ruining our towns. Only last night their -- Vitez was shelled and eight children died as a result. You spoke about the attack on Vitez. Isn't that what this document shows?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that's precisely what the document shows but the disaster that was yet to follow was even worse than the one you've just described as the year was nearing its end. We have not yet addressed Vares, Buhine Kuce, Krezancevo Celo, the worst was yet to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, I will have to ask you to tell us what you know about this. I believe we have that much time left. It would be quite precious to us. Let us try to round this off because all these topics are very important for us. Can we please now look at two army documents that date back to this period. We have been telling the Chamber a little bit what was going on in Kakanj and Bugojno but now let's move on to two army documents describing the position of the Croats in the area at the time. The next document is 2D 00438, 438. This is a document of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Supreme Command Staff Forward Command Post, information on civilians being exchanged in the Travnik area submitted to the supreme command staff in Sarajevo and also to the attention of the president of the Presidency. Commission members signing this document, I will be showing you some parts of the document that are very important. The commission for releasing prisoners based on an agreement signed on the 6th of October 1993 today visited the village of Skradno Busovaca municipality and the village of Mehurici Travnik municipality. The following was ascertained: In the village of Skradno, there were 45 local refugees and 90 refugees from Velika Bukovica, these are Muslim refugees. It is not unimportant because we know that there were Muslim refugees as well but let me take you to paragraph 2. In the village of may Mehurici we found 247 Croat civilians who were put up in a school gym. They are under the protection of the military police of the 306th Brigade but they are receiving death threats from the so-called Brigade of Death mostly consisting of Mujahedin foreigners based nearby. Mr. Salko Beba from Operation Group West, who was escorting us told us that the day before we arrived, these Mujahedin shot about 50 civilians in a nearby village. A single civilian survived. The execution is now among those 47 -- 247 civilians at Mehurici and then it goes on to say that one of members of the 36th brigade in Mehurici told them that the Mujahedin were also mistreating the local Muslims. The next paragraph reads, we are of the opinion that the Mujahedin problem makes the already complex relations between the Muslims and the Croats even more complex in the area of responsibility of the 3rd corps. The president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina along with the commander of the BH army should go to Zenica or should have the 3rd Corps commander over to Sarajevo for urgent consultations in order to deal with these problems. The last paragraph reads, between Mr. Salko Beba, Mr. Petar Skopljak, the representatives of the HVO, there was an agreement that the next day of the 14th of June there should be an exchange of civilians between the village of Skradno and civilians from the village of Mehurici. We are conscious that this is a textbook case of ethnic cleansing, but we are unable to provide any other sort of protection for these civilians in order to keep them from annihilation. We, the members of this commission, agree that this exchange should take place. This is a document that -- where the BH army is telling us what is going on. The date is the 23rd of June. Please let's not comment on this because the next document I have is a mere continuation of this document. The document that I am talking about is 2D 686 and then I will be asking a couple of questions about this. Can you tell me first and this is something I've been mentioning a lot in courtroom, and it would be good for the benefit of the Chamber but for you to tell us. You know who Stjepan Siber was, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. The same as Jovan Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The 25th of June 1993, in this document, he claims he is the deputy commander and that's the capacity in which he signed this document, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Divjak and he were both, and I'm not certain about this, assistants or deputies. I'm not sure what it was that was called at the time but they were the -- some of the top men in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This document was obviously put together by him and he delivers this document a mere two days later following this document by the exchange commission, he submits this to the president and to the commander of the Supreme Command staff of the BH army personally at least that's what it says, personally as well. He refers to a 15th of June document, he says, "I remain adamant about your visit to Zenica." The document is -- I'm sorry, my colleague is drawing my attention to this, I know that everybody's got this, but the number is 2D 002686. If you look at paragraph 2, this is an integral report and I will be quoting some things that I believe are important. Paragraph 2, the 26th of May, the president of the municipal authorities Dzaferovic Ramiz faced Siber Kraic and Vranj, and he says as a citizen, I feel I've been let down by the 3rd corps and the top leadership of the 3rd Corps is heavily involved in a crime and robbery. There are some people there who are executing other people after acts of robbery and then let's move on to paragraph 3. Merdan is the main organizer of the religious units known as Suvalic and Puric's the 7th Muslim Brigade. Then we skip another one, another line I think this is the most important thing, and then I think you spoke about this it reads, holding sway over Zenica and the 3rd corps our commanders who are steeped in crime. They don't want to be the Chetniks because they do not derive any benefit from that situation. At the same time, clashes with the HVO are very much in their best interest. I'm skipping to the next page in Croatian. On the 8th of June 1993, 35 Croats were shot in the village of Bikosi. Four witnesses were wounded and remained alive. They were shot by the Mujahedin. On the 10th of June 1993, over 30 Croats were shot in the village of Susanj near Ovnak by some army. On the 22nd June 1992 [as interpreted], members of the commission for the release of prisoners, Alihodzic and Negovetic spoke to Salko Beba from OG West only to find out the following then he goes on to describe something and we've been reading that about in the previous documents. I'm not going to repeat that now. He goes on to say everything that we've read already about the shootings and the capture of Croat civilians. Then he goes on and says we would like to emphasise the commander this crime and robbery are our rife. Fighters coming back from further afield are bringing their bags back full and as soon as they see that there is nothing to rob, loot, or take in an area they refuse to go there. The military police of the 36th brigade goes on to say the police from some of the brigades continue to arrest civilians and they beat them up in cellars all over the place. These security service is not cooperating at all which is something that Mr. Ganic could see for himself when he met with the 3rd Corps on the 15th of May 1993. The 22nd of June, 1992, it should be the 22nd of June 1993, that's correct and the page is 88, line 4. Sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just add, you gave a number which I think is not the right number. The right number is 2D 00686. You have added a 2 which is not part of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I don't think I did. It must have been an error in the transcript. It's 2D 00686.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, first let me ask you this generally speaking, these are BH army documents. Were you familiar with this situation that was in progress in the area, the offences committing against the Croats. How informed about this were you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This type of information was available to us at the time, it was available to me personally. I can say that the BH army was predominantly made up of Muslims. There were soldiers there from various parts of the former Yugoslavia and from abroad as well. I don't know if I said this but I might as well say this, both Mr. Ganic and Mr. Halilovic are from Sandzak. We call them Sandzaklija, the Sandzak people. There were some from Montenegro. There were some who perhaps weren't aware of how sensitive the relations between the various ethnicities over where I come from were and here I'm referring primarily to the Mujahedin. The criminal offences described here don't as a matter of fact reflect what I heard was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were subjected to the worst imaginable kind of torture and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript and in order to avoid further interventions you are saying does not quite reflect everything but I want to know if you know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note could the speakers please be asked to speak one at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about these events reflected in these two documents? Were you aware of these events?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me now return to a term that you used. You talked about the Croats leaving the area at the time. We have to be very specific about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you a follow-up question based on the previous two documents. Witness, we have just seen two documents. I knew about those documents. One of those documents is addressed to the Supreme Command of the army in Sarajevo and to the president of the Presidency. I'm talking about document 2D 438. The second document is 2D 686, it is also addressed to the same people. Those documents clearly show that members of the ABiH army talk about misdeeds committed by the ABiH which shows that the situation is very complicated, indeed. 2D 686 which was drafted by Siber mentions problems. The other document which was also drafted by Ivan Negovetic and Fadil Alihodzic mentions the situation in Mehurici. You stated that you were aware of the situation but from where you stood, did you know that within the command of the ABiH, maybe not everybody agreed. There was no unity. Some people seemed to challenge certain actions so did you know about those discords within the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot be a reliable witness on this but on the basis of the documents and the knowledge that we had, we in the Presidency -- we can conclude that there was some discord. That means that from the -- that it would depend on the leadership of that specific brigade or corps how they would act. I told you yesterday, Your Honours, that it seems to me that the 3rd Corps was the most extremist one and that it committed the worst crimes against Croats, and I believe that this is the corps that is referred to here. So in the army leadership in Sarajevo, these developments could be observed, and I myself spoke at the Presidency meetings. I said, "If you're on the top of a hill, you can push a stone, make it roll down the hill but you cannot control it anymore once you do that." I think that some of the BH army units were no longer under control, what little control there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is your answer, so according to you, some ABiH elements escaped control including control by the Presidency; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my assumption or rather this is my assessment not my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica. Sorry for interrupting you, but I wanted to talk about those two documents before we move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Questions were of assistance I'm not quite finished with those two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As a follow-up to the question by His Honour Judge Antonetti who asked but members of the BH army I would like us to go back to the civilians, Croats, people living in that area. Are they moving out, fleeing, or are they being evicted from that area regardless of who is actually doing that? Either members of the BH army who are under the control of the BH army or some other uncontrolled elements. The reason why I am going back to this is because you say that the Croat people moved out of this area so could you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat people from Central Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat his answer, it was not quite clear to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The question is why did they move out?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They moved out under the pressure and because of the threat of the BH army and other Muslim forces that are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please go on? I just wanted to clear this up and could you please continue now.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So some people moved out to Herzegovina. Others move out again under the same pressure to other places where the war was not so prevalent at that time so for instance they moved to Kiseljak from Kakanj they moved through Kraljeva Sutjeska to Vares and then again they moved out of Vares to Herzegovina. My brother lived in Vares with his family. My wife, in fact, is from Vares, but she did not live in Vares at that time. My brother moved out of Vares and moved to Herzegovina. Grave crimes were committed there and huge masses of population, I cannot give you the exact figures now, but we're talking about tens of thousands of people moving out. They moved out under the pressure engendered by the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akmadzic for being so specific. This is what I sought. Now I would like to move on to another topic. I will try to deal with it by 7.00 but I will be guided by the Trial Chamber. If I don't finish it by 7.00 I can either go on until I finish it or do it tomorrow. In early 1993, Mr. Akmadzic, you were the prime minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now we will be dealing with the topic of arming of the BH army and the HVO the way they procured the arms at that time and before that time and even after that time period.
